questions.prompt: Kayla starts her first job. Her employer asks her to fill out Form W-4. What is it used for?

choices.text: To apply for a Social Security number
To report her yearly wages to the IRS
To sign up for health insurance
To set her federal income tax withholding

questions.correct_answer: To set her federal income tax withholding
questions.intro: Form W-4 (Employee's Withholding Certificate) tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. You fill it out when you start a job and can update it any time, such as after a second job begins or your situation changes.
questions.feedback: The W-4 sets federal income tax withholding.
questions.topic: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2

misconceptions.A: Confuses the W-4 with an SSN application
misconceptions.B: Confuses the W-4 with the W-2
misconceptions.C: Confuses tax forms with benefit forms

questions.prompt: On her W-4, Kayla asks for $20 of extra withholding per paycheck. She is paid biweekly. How much extra will be withheld over a full year?
questions.intro: Step 4(c) of Form W-4 lets you request extra withholding each pay period. Multiply by the number of paychecks in a year to see the yearly effect.
questions.feedback: Biweekly = 26 paychecks: $20 × 26 = $520.
questions.topic: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2

questions.prompt: It is February 15, and Ana still has not received last year's Form W-2 from her employer. What is true?

choices.text: It is late; she should contact the employer
It is on time; W-2s are due by April 15
It is on time; W-2s are due by June 30
She should skip filing this year without it

questions.correct_answer: It is late; she should contact the employer
questions.intro: Form W-2 (Wage and Tax Statement) reports a worker's wages for the year and the taxes withheld. Employers generally must send it by January 31 (or the next business day if that falls on a weekend or holiday), and employees use it to file their tax returns.
questions.feedback: W-2s are generally due by January 31, so a missing W-2 in mid-February is late; ask the employer, and the IRS can help if it still does not arrive.
questions.topic: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2

misconceptions.B: Confuses the W-2 deadline with the tax filing deadline
misconceptions.D: Ignores that she can request it and still file

questions.prompt: The U.S. income tax is "pay-as-you-go." What does this mean for employees?

choices.text: Tax is paid once, only when you retire
Only people who ask to pay tax have to pay it
Tax is paid only by employers, never employees
Tax is paid gradually through paycheck withholding during the year

questions.correct_answer: Tax is paid gradually through paycheck withholding during the year
questions.intro: Federal income tax is collected throughout the year. For employees, the employer withholds part of each paycheck and sends it to the government on the employee's behalf.
questions.feedback: Withholding spreads tax payments over the year.

questions.prompt: Last year Kayla received a $1,300 refund. She had no refundable credits or other tax payments; her refund came only from paycheck withholding. What does that tell her?

choices.text: She earned a $1,300 bonus from the IRS
Her employer underpaid her by $1,300
She owes $1,300 more next year
She had $1,300 more withheld than her tax

questions.correct_answer: She had $1,300 more withheld than her tax
questions.intro: A refund is the amount by which your payments and refundable credits are more than your tax. Payments include withholding and estimated tax. When a refund comes only from withholding, it is your own overpaid tax coming back, not extra income, and you could have had more in each paycheck.
questions.feedback: With no refundable credits or other payments, the refund is overpaid withholding being returned.
questions.topic: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2

misconceptions.A: Treats a refund as free money

questions.prompt: Kayla starts a second part-time job. Why might her withholding now be too low?

choices.text: Two jobs always get the correct combined withholding automatically
Part-time jobs are not taxed
Her first employer stops withholding
Each employer withholds as if that job were her only income

questions.correct_answer: Each employer withholds as if that job were her only income
questions.intro: When you have more than one job, each employer's payroll may assume its pay is your only income, so total withholding can fall short. Step 2 of Form W-4 addresses multiple jobs.
questions.feedback: Each payroll ignores the other job, so combined income can be under-withheld. Updating the W-4 (Step 2) fixes this.

misconceptions.A: Thinks withholding adds up correctly automatically

questions.prompt: Under IRS rules, who may claim exemption from federal income tax withholding on Form W-4?

choices.text: Someone who owed no tax last year and expects none this year
Anyone under age 21
Anyone who works part time while attending high school
Anyone who wants a larger paycheck

questions.correct_answer: Someone who owed no tax last year and expects none this year
questions.intro: You may claim "exempt" on Form W-4 only if you had no federal income tax liability last year and expect none this year. Exemption affects federal income tax withholding only, not Social Security or Medicare.
questions.feedback: Both conditions must be met: no liability last year and none expected this year.

questions.prompt: IRS rules allow claiming exempt only with no income tax liability last year and none expected this year. Jamal owed no federal income tax last year. This year, with a full-time job, he expects to have a positive federal income tax liability. Should he claim exempt?

choices.text: Yes, because he owed nothing last year
Yes, because he is a new worker
Yes, so that he can get a bigger refund next spring
No; he expects to owe income tax this year

questions.correct_answer: No; he expects to owe income tax this year
questions.feedback: Both conditions must hold. He expects a tax liability this year, so he cannot claim exempt. (Liability is the tax itself, not the amount due when filing.)

misconceptions.A: Uses only one of the two conditions
